passage: The Reyes group compared two receptor proteins, A and B, that bind a steroid ligand with different affinities. Purified protein was held at 1 nM, a concentration far below either dissociation constant, so that the free ligand concentration was approximately equal to the total added. Ligand was titrated over a wide range, and the fraction of protein with bound ligand was measured by fluorescence anisotropy after each addition reached equilibrium. Each binding curve was hyperbolic and showed no evidence of cooperativity. The researchers intend to use the receptor with the tighter binding as a biosensor, and they want to know what ligand concentration would be required to saturate it at 80% occupancy. All measurements were made at 25 °C in identical buffer. Protein stocks were centrifuged before use to remove aggregates, and ligand stocks were verified by absorbance. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

questions.stem: At [ligand] = 100 nM, what is the fraction of protein A bound?
questions.explanation: Fraction bound = [L]/(Kd + [L]) = 100/(20+100) = 0.83. The B column gives 0.33.
questions.trap: Students read the B column (0.33) or the protein A value at a different ligand concentration (0.71 at 50 nM, 0.91 at 200 nM) instead of 0.83 at 100 nM.

questions.stem: Why was protein held far below the Kd?

options.A: So that cooperativity can be detected
options.B: So that ligand depletion by binding is negligible and free ligand ≈ total ligand
options.C: So that Kd equals the protein concentration
options.D: So that the protein is certain to be fully saturated

questions.explanation: If protein were comparable to Kd, binding would deplete free ligand and distort the fit to the simple hyperbola.
questions.trap: Students think a very low protein concentration saturates the protein or reveals cooperativity, but it only keeps free ligand approximately equal to total ligand.

questions.stem: What ligand concentration is needed for 80% occupancy of the higher-affinity protein (Kd = 20 nM)?
questions.trap: Students pick 20 nM (half-saturation) or mis-scale Kd to 40 or 160 nM; 80% occupancy requires [L] = 4 x Kd = 80 nM.

options.A: Protein A binds the ligand with higher affinity than protein B
options.B: Kd equals the ligand concentration at half-saturation
options.C: A lower Kd means lower affinity
options.D: A hyperbolic curve is consistent with noncooperative binding

questions.explanation: Kd is inversely related to affinity: a smaller Kd means tighter binding.
questions.trap: Students assume a lower Kd means lower affinity because 'lower' sounds weaker, but Kd is a dissociation constant, so a smaller Kd means tighter binding.

questions.stem: Which protein behavior differs from these hyperbolic curves?

options.A: Binding of a single ligand to one site on a monomeric protein
options.D: Hemoglobin's sigmoidal oxygen binding due to cooperativity

questions.explanation: Hemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively (Hill coefficient > 1), giving a sigmoidal curve, while myoglobin is hyperbolic like proteins A and B.
questions.trap: Students pick monomeric single-site binding, Michaelis–Menten saturation or myoglobin because they sound like binding curves, but those are hyperbolic like A and B; only cooperative hemoglobin is sigmoidal.
